state: one rung measured; the remaining rungs do not reach a steady state under this solver configuration

measured.grid: TMR-distributed 113x33 C-grid (3584 cells), converted from the published PLOT3D file

reference.note: Published values are finest-grid (897x257) only; a single coarse rung supports no comparison claim and none is made
reference.source: turbmodels.larc.nasa.gov NACA 0012 validation, CFL3D SST on the 897x257 grid with point-vortex farfield correction (n0012clcd_cfl3d_sst.dat via mirror tmbwg.github.io/turbmodels, retrieved 2026-07-25); FUN3D values from the same validation page

pending: A steady or time-averaged closure for the medium and fine rungs at every alpha; until then no ladder, no observed order, no card change
deviations: Incompressible simpleFoam analog of the M=0.15 case
No point-vortex farfield correction; the grids place the farfield near 500 chords, and the outer pressure is pinned uniform there
The TMR coarse grid's own wall spacing gives max y+ near 10 at this Reynolds number; that is the reference family's coarse rung, not a choice of ours
Grids are the TMR point files themselves, converted with plot3dToFoam; the wake cut closes through the converter's point merge
findings_2026_07_25: Alpha 10, 225x65 grid: a sustained force oscillation under second-order momentum advection at two relaxation levels (16000 and 24000 iteration budgets); the swing grows and shrinks with a period of thousands of iterations and never decays
Alpha 0, 113x33 grid: the same oscillation, antisymmetric (Cl swings of 0.3 on a symmetric case)

Root cause isolated by scheme substitution on the alpha 0 rung: first-order momentum is perfectly steady (Cd 0.0229, overdiffused and not usable for verification), TVD limitedLinear reduces the cycle to about 3e-4 around Cd 0.0090 but never flattens over 15000 iterations; the feedback lives in the wake and trailing-edge convection

The published CFL3D results converge the same grids with a compressible implicit solver and different numerical dissipation; a time-accurate solve with averaged coefficients, or a dissipation study, is the honest next step
